title: Ziryab the musician
hook: a musician from Baghdad who brought new music, food and fashion to Cordoba

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abbas ibn Firnas, who tied on wings, jumped, and landed hard for want of a tail. Your line was: he tried to fly. What new thing did you try, and what would you change next time? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

Soup first. Then the meat. Then something sweet to finish. A meal in courses, in a set order, on a table that might have glass on it instead of gold. In the stories of al-Andalus, that order at dinner is credited to one man, and he wasn't a cook. He was a singer from Baghdad with an oud on his back. People called him Ziryab. He came west to Cordoba, and the reports say the city started eating, dressing and even cutting its hair the way he did. Today: Ziryab the musician.
screen: `SOUP, MEAT, THEN SWEETS.` → `A SINGER FROM BAGHDAD.` → `CORDOBA FOLLOWS HIS LEAD.`

segments.voice: The story comes to us mostly through the historian al-Maqqari, gathering older accounts. In Baghdad, it says, Ziryab studied music under a famous master, Ishaq al-Mawsili. The student became too good. When he sang before the caliph, his teacher grew jealous and told him, in effect, to leave or face trouble. So Ziryab went west, and in Cordoba the emir Abd al-Rahman the Second welcomed him into his court. Then come the reports, a long list of them. He added a string to the oud. He played with a plectrum made from an eagle's quill instead of wood. He opened a school of music. And off the stage: meals served in courses, glass vessels on the table, clothes changed with the seasons, a new way to wear the hair. Historians read that list carefully. Some of it may be praise piled on a famous name. But the picture of a court learning taste from one gifted person holds together. So why does a Muslim path spend a day on a singer? Partly because Muslim scholars differ over music, and that's worth saying plainly: some permit instruments, some don't, and others draw lines in between. And partly for a hadith. Sahih Muslim records that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warned against pride, and a man asked: what if someone likes his clothes to be fine and his sandals good? The answer, in substance: God is beautiful and loves beauty; pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Care for how things look and taste was never the problem in that answer. Contempt was. That fits the week we've walked: knowledge as worship, Tariq's mountain, Cordoba and its mosque, a caliph, a man with wings, and now a man with manners. Music and manners.
screen: `A JEALOUS TEACHER IN BAGHDAD.` · `A NEW LIFE AT CORDOBA'S COURT.` · `A STRING, A QUILL, A MEAL IN COURSES.` · `GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.` · then, large: `MUSIC AND MANNERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to share a new recipe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one dish you love that someone close to you has never had. Maybe a grandmother's, maybe a street food, maybe something you made once and got right. Picture it in order: what goes in first, what it smells like, what it looks like on the plate. Now think of one person to share it with, by cooking it or just by sending the recipe. If you pray, you can give thanks for the food in the words you already know. If you don't, simply notice the gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Ziryab the musician. The singer from Baghdad who, by the reports, taught Cordoba new music, new meals and new manners. Today's word.
Your line: music and manners. Today, share one recipe with someone, and set one meal out with a little care, even if it's just a clean plate and a quiet minute. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Ziryab in Baghdad. you've just sung well before the caliph, and your own teacher, jealous, tells you to leave or face trouble. what do you do?
options: stay and fight for your place at court.
leave Baghdad and take your music west.
fork.reveal: by al-Maqqari's account he left, and in Cordoba the emir Abd al-Rahman the Second took him in. the teacher's jealousy sent the music to Spain.
